question.:question/worked-solution:
If we write the integrand as a power of $x$, we have ${x}^{0}=1.$ Therefore, we can use the power rule with $n=0$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 1\,\text{d}x & =\int {x}^{0}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{0+1}}{0+1}+C \\  & =x+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's check by differentiating:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x+C) & = \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x)+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(C) & = \\ 1+0 & = \\ 1\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
We apply the power rule with $n=1$, and we get

$$
\int {x}^{1}\,\text{d}x=\frac{{x}^{1+1}}{1+1}+C=\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+C.
$$

Let's check by differentiating:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+C) & = \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{{x}^{2}}{2})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(C) & = \\ \frac{1}{2}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2})+0 & = \\ \frac{1}{2}\cdot 2{x}^{1} & = \\ {x}^{1}\,✓\end{aligned}
$$
